title: Friend recalls fatal night: Officer apologized for shooting teen
article: Keyvan Tabesh was riding an emotional roller coaster the night he was shot to death by a Port Moody cop, a friend told an inquest yesterday.
One minute, he was crying in a coffee shop, unable to accept that he had almost struck a girl, his friend Amir Aghaei testified.
The girl was the driver of a car whose window Tabesh had smashed out with a machete a few minutes earlier for no reason.
The next minute Tabesh, 18, was barrelling down the main street of Port Moody at up to 180 km/h, trying to elude police.
"We're all going to die. We're all going to die. We're all going to die," Aghaei quoted his friend as saying as they raced down St. John Street at 1:45 a.m. on July 14, 2003.
"He had been committed \[to a mental institution\] a few months before," Aghaei told the inquest in New Westminster.
As they sat in a coffee shop after the window-smashing incident, Aghaei said his friend could not be consoled.
"I never saw him so sad before," Aghaei said.
"I hugged him. I said, 'Please don't drive.' He said, 'You don't understand my pain.'
"I said, 'I do I do.'
"He said, 'I almost hit a girl.'"
Tabesh, who was taking medication for his mental condition, insisted on driving a third friend home. As they drove along
St. John, Tabesh noticed the woman he had terrified a half-hour earlier at a gas station.
Aghaei said Tabesh pulled into the gas station to apologize.
Aghaei noticed a police car and Tabesh sped off.
He turned down Electronic Avenue, a dead end. He made a U-turn and was confronted by the police car at the entrance to the street and stopped his car, facing it.
"I told him, 'No no no. Don't make any mistake," said Aghaei.
Tabesh hit the gas and sped past the police car.
He stopped in a dark cul-de-sac in the 2100-block St. George Street, where the shooting took place.
Aghaei said they thought the plainclothes officer in an unmarked police car, a gold Mazda, was a neighbour.
He said the Mazda backed up about eight metres and stopped with the headlights shining on them.
All that time, Aghaei said he was trying to calm his friend. He said Tabesh grabbed the machete and ran at the Mazda.
"I tried to catch him with my hand," said Aghaei.
"When he got to one metre \[from the Mazda\] I heard, 'Stop!' and then there was the gun."
Aghaei said he heard three shots, the second one hitting him in the leg.
"I saw Keyvan under the car, his head moving back and forth. He said, 'Oh God.'"
As Aghaei lay on the wet pavement, the officer came over and put his hand on Aghaei's head.
"He said, 'You were so close to me. Sorry I shot you,'" testified Aghaei.
The officer, whose identity can't be published by court order because of threats to him and his family, is to testify today.
